column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article gives his command as legatus of Lusitania 'between 26 BC and 22 BC'; the entry says legate in Hispania Ulterior and dates him fl. 25-22 BCE. I gave only the end of his command (22 BCE) and the province as the article names it.
The article's Latin inscription is garbled ('Dulce et Decori est pro patria mori'); I gave its meaning in English rather than quote it.

The article calls him 'the first dewan of Mysore from 1782 to 1811'; the entry describes him as head of finance under Hyder and Tipu and made diwan by the British after 1799. I said he took the title of Dewan under Tipu, as the article's body says, without the 1782-1811 span. The article also says Robert Frykenberg suggests Arthur Wellesley learned the use of cavalry from Purnaiah; left out for length.

The article's account of the succession is garbled ('When the second Umayyad caliph died, and his brother was assassinated after his death'); I kept only Ibn Hayyan's two factions at al-Hakam II's death and did not say what became of al-Mughira. Anderson names the commissioner as 'al-Mushtaq, consort of Abd al-Rahman III', the same woman the article earlier calls the concubine Mushtaq; I wrote 'his mother'. Left out: the Pyxis of Zamora comparison and Prado-Vilar's fertility reading of the date palm.

SKIPPED: article too thin: under 250 words of substance (founding date, the name's origin, a hospital, a rural conflict over stock theft) The article says the town was founded in 1876 and that King Mhlontlo of the amaMpondomise was accused of killing the magistrate Hamilton Hope; it does not mention Cape annexation or the magistracy as the entry does.

The article says he 'captured Johor Lama on 1717 without the help of the Bugis', but elsewhere dates his attack on Johor to February 1718 and the capture of the capital to 1 March 1718, as the entry does. I left the 1717 date out. The 1721 battle with Daeng Parani (muskets and blunderbusses against swords and cannon) is left out for length.

The article gives his reign as 1216-1246 and his death as 1260, with Rajendra III succeeding in 1246; the entry gives r. 1216-1256. I gave no end date and no date for Rajendra's succession. The article contradicts itself on the civil war: it says it ended 'with the former killing the latter', yet quotes Rajendra's inscriptions boasting that he 'killed Rajaraja after making him wear the double crown for three years', and also gives Rajaraja's death as 1260. I mentioned only the civil war. The article gives no date for the capture by Kopperunchinga; the entry says around 1231.

The article gives his reign as 1629-1687 in the lead and says he succeeded in 1634 (1629 in some sources); the entry says king from 1635. I gave no accession year. The article mentions the 1638 treaty with Westerwolt 'by 23 May 1638'; the entry already covers the 1638 treaty, so I did not repeat it.

SKIPPED: article too thin (most of it is empty lists of judges) and its history contradicts the entry on the court's seat and the Jaipur bench The entry says the court was inaugurated in August 1949 with its principal seat at Jodhpur and a permanent bench at Jaipur. The article says it was founded at Jaipur, inaugurated there by the Rajpramukh Maharaja Sawai Man Singh on 29 August 1949, and moved to Jodhpur after the integration of Rajasthan in 1956 on the Satyanarayan Rao committee's recommendation; it also says a Jaipur bench was formed on 31 January 1977 and, in the same sentence, 'dissolved in 1958'. The entry's account of the seat needs a second source. Other facts in the article: the Rajasthan High Court Ordinance, 1949 united five earlier high courts (Jodhpur, Jaipur, Bikaner, the former Rajasthan and Matsya Union); the first Chief Justice was Kamalkanta Verma; new premises on the outskirts of Jodhpur opened in 2019; a statue of Manu installed on 3 March 1989 has been the subject of protests and legal challenges.

The article's opening says the title existed 'from India's independence in 1947 until 1956'; its own account and the entry date the first Rajpramukh to 1948 (Madhya Bharat). I left out the 1947 start. The article spells the Maharana of Udaipur both 'Bhopal Singh' and 'Bhupal Singh'; I gave only his title.

The entry places the mound in the Nawalparasi district; the article says Parasi District (Ramgram Municipality). I named only the municipality. The article calls the Koliyas a kingdom (mahājanapada); the entry calls them a clan republic. I wrote 'peoples' and 'a major Koliya town'. The article gives the stupa as 7 metres high and the stupa complex as 10 m high and 23.5 m in diameter; I gave the mound's dimensions only, as the complex's.

The article is inconsistent on his first term as Amatya: 'from 1674 to 1680' in the lead and 'until 1678' in the body; it also says he was '22-23 years old' at the 1674 coronation, which does not fit a birth in 1650. I gave neither the end of the term nor his age. The lead calls him regent to four later kings; the body gives the regency only under Rajaram (1689-1698) and Sambhaji II (from 1714). I followed the body. The article spells the fort Gingee; the entry writes Jinji.

The article says ore mining in the Old Bed began in the Bronze Age, but also that the earliest mining activity occurred in the late 7th century AD; the entry says from at least the 10th century. I gave no start date. The article says Henry II had the Imperial Palace of Goslar built in 1005 and the Salians Conrad II and Henry III extended it; the entry says the Salian emperors built it. I left the palace out. The article says control of the mine passed in 1552 to the Margraviate of Brandenburg, then that Duke Henry V of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel seized it in 1552; I followed the second, fuller account.

The article says the Pehuenche advance into Mamül Mapu took place between 1775 and 1790, consistent with the entry's 18th-century formation. Nothing in the article about Calfucurá or Mansilla, which the entry names.

The article gives his force leaving Jodhpur as 100 horsemen and 500 foot-soldiers, then says he 'led an army of around 300 of his clansmen'. I gave no numbers. The article does not date the founding of the city of Bikaner; the entry gives 1488.

The entry says the town grew from an Iron Age settlement and a Roman fort; the article says there is minimal evidence of a fort (a single V-shaped ditch on the island between the river channels) and that a fort around AD 50 'cannot be ruled out'. I left the fort out.

The entry says Alauddin besieged Chittor 'for about eight months'; the article gives only two months of unsuccessful siege before the bombardment and the capture on 26 August 1303. I gave no total length. Kakka Suri also says Alauddin 'made him move like a monkey from one city to another', which Dasharatha Sharma takes to mean he survived the siege; the entry dates his death to 1303. I left the survival reading out. The article gives 1359 VS for the Dariba inscription; 1302 CE as given.

The article says the audiencia began functioning in 1543; the entry says it was installed in Lima in 1544. I gave no date for its opening. The article ends the court in 1821; the entry says 'the 1820s'. 1821 given as the article states, which falls within the entry's wording.
The entry's figures for inflation (over 2,000 per cent in 1993, single figures within a few years) are not in the article; nothing on them added.
The lead gives two phases, 1721-1725 and 1730-1735; the entry's 1721-1735 span covers both. The article spells the governor of Buenos Aires Zavala; the name is left out of the text.

The entry says the Confederation built new fortresses at Ulm and Rastatt; the article says Frederick William IV proposed improvements to the fortifications of Mainz, Ulm and Rastatt, and Bavaria built Germersheim. Ulm and Rastatt left out of the text.
The article gives her birth as 3 or 6 March 1497 and her death as 13 or 16 June 1553; exact days left out. Alberico's elevation to Prince of Massa in 1568 is in the entry only.
The article says nothing of Rendlesham or Sutton Hoo; the early medieval history is in the entry only. Article thin on history; text kept short.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words and adds little beyond the entry
Article thin (about 340 words); text kept to two sections. The article also calls him Mohammed Sayyid, the last Mughal governor; left out as unclear.
The article says the former (Saguamanchica) won at Chocontá; the sentence is unclear and the outcome is left out.

SKIPPED: different subject: the entry is a twelfth-century drought tied to the decline of the Ghana Empire; the article is about Sahel droughts in general from the 17th century on and says nothing of the twelfth century or Ghana
The article does not name the author of the long quoted raid account; summarised as a contemporary account.
SKIPPED: different subject: the article is the namesake Sakai Tadakatsu of Obama (1587-1662), roju and lord of Kawagoe and Obama; the entry is the Sakai Tadakatsu (1594-1647) moved to Shonai in 1622
SKIPPED: article under 250 words; beyond the entry it adds only the family's line of prime ministers and the museum's opening in 1968
SKIPPED: article about 300 words, and it disagrees with the entry: born 1594 (entry 1602) and Angola and Sao Tome regained in 1647 (entry: Luanda retaken in 1648)
Article: Méstwin II last Duke 1270-1294; entry agrees on 1294.

Article calls Sarahan a small town; the entry a village: neither word used. Article spells the river Satluj and the kingdom Bushahr (entry: Sutlej, Bashahr). 'Resurrected' in the article rendered as restored.
Article gives two dates for the start of Samtskhe's independence: 1268 (lead, first sovereign prince) and 1266 (injü status from Hulagu). Neither year given in the text.

Article dates the reign c. 1355 - c. 1397 (Seii died around 1355; Bunei took the throne around 1397); entry gives 1350-1395. No reign years given in the text. Entry places Kume near Naha; article says Kumemura, founded 1392, was adjacent to Shuri. Left out.

Article: about 581 Trelawny Maroons transported to Nova Scotia (58 stayed in Jamaica); entry: about 600. Number left out. Article says the Maroons travelled to Freetown 'at the start of the nineteenth century'; entry says 1800. No year given in the text. Article calls the end a 'bloody stalemate' and says the Maroons 'surrendered in December 1795'; worded as agreeing terms.
Entry says Goryeo gained the land east of the Yalu; article speaks of the land south of the Yalu (Sŏ lamented that the Jurchens allowed Goryeo only that). Direction left out.

Article says Beomnang (fl. 632-646), a student of the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin, first brought the teaching to Korea, which is earlier than the entry's 'eighth and ninth centuries'. Beomnang and his dates left out; Sinhaeng's dates (704-779) also left out to avoid the point. Article's claim that the Nine Mountain Schools 'adopted the name Jogye Order in 826' sits oddly with its other statements (first record of the Nine Mountains 1084; Jogye predominant from Jinul's time): left out.

The article's passage on medical research is muddled: it places autopsies at Field Hospital XII on the island but also says 'this work was performed at the camp at Swakopmund', and garbles a sentence naming Eugen Fischer and Hugo Bofinger. Neither doctor named; worded generally. Article gives the camp's closing as April 1907; entry dates 1905-1907, consistent.

Article contradicts itself on his death: 25 September 1660 in the lead, 1663-64 in the body. Entry gives d. 1660 and reign to 1660. No death year given in the text. Entry calls him 'the greatest ruler'; not repeated. Article says Soma Shekhar 'was murdered by his Brahmins': the murderers left out as unclear.
Article: the Komet is 'multi-centennial', which sits oddly with a 19th-20th-century sultan's belongings; age left out.
The article spells her name both Sibyl and Sybil; Sibyl used. 'Benevolent dictator' not used in own voice.
Article is short (about 300 words), much of it repeating the entry; the text may fall near the lower limit.
Article gives his birth as 363 (a year after Sima Yao) and death 3 February 403; entry dates 364-403. Birth year left out.
Article gives the 1956 workforce figures as quoted; only two of the four pairs used.

Article gives the tank two dates: built between 1731 and 1738, and built in 1733. No date given for the tank. The claim that the Sivadol is the tallest Shiva temple tower in India ('said to be') left out as a ranking.
SKIPPED: article has under 300 words, most of it already in the description

Article says the spin-off of the bank was mandated in 1935 but elsewhere that it was 'initiated in 1934' and that the Belgian bank was spun off in 1934 (head office section). Worded as 'in the 1930s'.

Sources in the article disagree about the battle on the Tungabhadra in c. 1059: Sastri counts it a Chalukya victory (marked by the Annigeri temple), Sen a defeat at Mudakkarru. The temple is told as built to mark a victory, as the article says; Sen's view left out. Chopra et al. place Kudalasangama at the confluence of the Krishna and Tungabhadra, others at Koodli: location left out.
Two sections: the article supports no third heading without repeating the entry.
The article mentions only Saipan among the Mariana islands; Tinian and Rota (in the entry) are not in it.
The article names both kings, Cleombrotus I and Agesilaus II, as supporting the acquittal; the entry names Agesilaus, which the article calls the decisive support.
The entry dates burial to around 870; the article says some time after 870-71, its latest coin from 870. I gave the building's and chest's dates only.

The article says the town was capital from 1634 until 1694 but also that Annapolis became the legislature's seat in 1695 and that Nicholson moved the capital in 1695; the entry says 1694. I gave no year for the move.

Msiri's son Masuka is named in the article as the one who shot Bodson; accounts of the killing come from Hamadi via Moloney, from Bodson via Bonchamps, and from Stairs' letter, which adds that Msiri's men had cocked their guns.
Left out the article's closing line attributing a tuberculosis diagnosis to Jan Długosz, who died in 1480, before these events: an evident slip in the article.
The article's figure of 9,345 million state peasants in 1858 is evidently a slip (9,345,000?); left out. Its allotment figures in acres are probably desyatinas; left out.

The article says the statute stayed in force until the Nationalist occupation of Catalonia in 1939 and also that Franco repealed it on 5 April 1938 in the area he held; I gave only the 1938 repeal, as in the entry.
The article describes the work as gold and enamel; the entry says gilded copper and enamel. I left the material out.

The article gives the Hundred Swiss as serving from 1490 in its lead but as created in 1480 by Louis XI in its body; I gave no founding year. Pontifical Guard founding (1506) is in the entry and not repeated.
The article does not name Maysalun; it says the kingdom ended after the French ultimatum of 17 July 1920 and Faisal's surrender.

The article calls the building an army base as well as a palace, and says the underground floors and tunnels were used as exits, while the 2015 survey found no tunnel; I reported both as the article does.

The article gives two birthplaces and dates (Ngāruawāhia c. 1822; Orongokoekoea c. 1825); I gave neither. The entry has c. 1822. The article says he sued for peace with George Grey at Pirongia in 1881, but its own account has Mair sent by Grey; I named only Mair.
The article says the saint was born in the mid-15th century; the entry calls him a 16th-century saint. I gave no dates for his life.
The article does not mention the tribute to Oyo continuing during his reign, nor a formal royal monopoly; I kept to its wording on the Yevogan and the slave trade's share of royal income.

The article gives his reign as 680–739 and his accession in 680; the entry's dates are 8th century and it places his rule in the early 8th century, so I gave no accession year. The article dates the Tang investiture to 719/720 (Kaiyuan 7); the entry says the 720s. I gave no year for the embassy.

The article says the capture of Indrapuri in May 1881 sparked the Aceh War, but also mentions earlier fighting in the 1870s; the entry speaks of his resistance in the Aceh War from the early 1880s. I did not say the capture began the war. The article says 'controuler'; written as controller. Entry says 'reportedly poisoned'; the article states the poisoning without a hedge.

The article dates the first Theriso assembly to February 1905 but the outbreak to 23 March [O.S. 10 March] 1905, and the declaration both to 10 March and to 11/24 March; I gave only the outbreak date. The article says Venizelos was called to Greece in 1909 in its lead but invited by King George I in 1910 in its aftermath; I gave only his seven terms between 1910 and 1933. The article calls Venizelos prime minister of autonomous Crete in its context section; the High Commissioner's 'ministers were in fact counselors', so I called him one of the prince's ministers.

The entry says the palace blends Dravidian and Islamic styles; the article says Tamil Nadu agencies call it Indo-Saracenic or Dravidian while art historians class it as Vijayanagara (Nayaka) style integrating Indo-Islamic influences. Worded to fit both.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance, much of it already in the description; it also contradicts itself (regency from 675 though the king died in 676-677)
The article calls Desi Sangye Gyatso the Ganden Phodrang 'Prime Minister'; written as regent (desi). If the checker objects, use 'prime minister'.

Giraldus says Ua Ruairc tried to kill de Lacy and FitzGerald after failed talks; the Annals of Tigernach name Eoan Mer, Richard de Clare the Younger and Domhnall son of Annach Ua Ruairc as his killers; the Four Masters name de Lacy and Domhnall. Kept to the parley, which fits the entry.

The article gives him as 14th daimyo (1849-1858) and 17th (1870-1880); the 1870-1880 term was left out to avoid confusion with 'Restoration' details the article lacks. The article's Chōshū paragraph names 'Yoshitaka' once, plainly a slip for Yoshikatsu.

The entry says Aztec lands here were assigned to Tlacopan and its Tepanec allies; the article does not mention this (it says Tenochtitlan administered the area directly). Left both out. Nevado de Toluca height given as 4,690 m and 4,600 m in the article; omitted.
The article's History section has a confused sentence calling Shearith Jacob/Shearith Israel the original congregation founded in 1654; left out.
The article says four Gallic coins were found but lists five (one Valens, three Arcadius, one Honorius); the count is left out. The article does not mention abandonment after the 5th century.
The article gives the signatories as fifty in the lead and fifty-nine in the Background section; the number is left out.

The entry says the treaty ended the Third Javanese War of Succession; the article dates the war 1749-57 and says the treaty did not end hostilities, as Raden Mas Said fought on. That point is left out. The article's Article 6 gives the compensation as '10,000 royalties' without a currency.
The article gives Article XVI's strip as 600 km and says it reached nearly to the Bolivian border; not used. The Hayes arbitration is named only in passing in the article.
The entry names the battle of Staraya Russa and an indemnity; the article mentions neither, so they are not repeated or contradicted.
The article's account of Demosthenes's law (2,000 names in 20 boards of 60) does not add up; not used.

The entry says he ruled from 1570; the article says 1572, when his father died, and also dates the capture of Thăng Long to 1571, before that. The year he took power is left out. The article's quoted tribute to him is unattributed, so not used.

The article gives his death as 14 February 1631 in the lead and 14 January 1631 in the text; only the year is printed. The article dates Tamenobu's death to 1607, while the Tsugaru Tamenobu entry has 1608; the year of Nobuhira's succession is left out. The article says the clan name was changed to Tsugaru after Sekigahara; the Tamenobu article and entry put it at the recognition of 1590. Left out.

The article's lead gives his death as 29 March 1607, while its text has him die in Kyoto in January of the year after his son's death in October 1607, i.e. 1608 (the entry's year). No date is printed. The article names the eldest son both Nobutatsu and Nobutake; the name is left out.

The article says that after the fall of the Takeda, Kawajiri Hidetaka ruled Kai from Tsutsujigasaki until Nobunaga's death, and that the site was abandoned only when Kōfu Castle was completed in 1594. The entry says it was abandoned after Katsuyori's move in 1581. The later use and the final abandonment are left out. Left out the stone Hello Kitty by the museum.
The entry says he took Sanaa and built up Ta'izz as a base; the article names Zabid as his base and mentions only the rebuilding of Ta'izz's fortress. No contradiction is printed.
Short article; the text keeps to what it gives.

The article dates the founding to 1487, when Ahmad Alaq gained independence from his brother Mahmud; the entry dates the split of the eastern khanate to around 1462. The founding year is left out. The article spells the founder both Ahmad Alaq and Ahmad Araq.

The article says Nearchus's expedition 'discovered' the island; written as reached. The entry says the island belonged to Seleucid trade networks; the article says it is not known whether Bahrain was part of the Seleucid Empire. Printed as the article hedges it, which does not deny trade links.
The article names the daughter who married Salim as Mani bai (Jodh bai) in one place, Jagat Gosain in Ziegler's account and Manavati Bai in the list of descendants; no name is printed.
The article says the Covenant was signed 'on and before 28 September 1912'; the entry says 'on and after'. The dates of signing are left out.

The article gives his birth as 1761 or 1762 in the lead and 1761 in the text; the entry has 1761. No birth year printed. The article reports both that he died in Balaken (buried in Car) and, after Bakikhanov, in Elisu; only Balaken and Bakikhanov's view of the cause are printed.

The article gives the crowd as 10,000 in one place and 10,000-12,000 in another; no figure is printed. The article names the author of the Memorial of Küsnacht as 'Dr. Ludwig Snellhalf', apparently a garbled form; the author is left unnamed.

The entry calls the manuscript the oldest dated work of Swahili literature; the article says one of the earliest known documents in Swahili. Neither claim is repeated. The entry gives the other name Chuo cha Tambuka; the article has Kyuo kya Hereḳali. Only the article's names are printed.

The article's text names Siladitya VII as the last known ruler, while its list ends with Siladitya VI; neither is printed as the last. The article's text has a slip ('Dharasena II was succeeded by another son of Kharagraha I', meaning Dharasena III); the succession is not traced there.
Left out the claim that he offered the Thihoshin Pagoda image to the Burmese king Alaungsithu, which sits oddly with the rest of the article.
SKIPPED: article too short: about 250 words of substance, under the length a longer text needs The article gives the length as 87 km; the entry says about 90 km.

The article gives the volok as about 21.38 hectares in its lead, 30 morgs (21.3 hectares) on Bona's estates and 33 morgs (23.5 hectares) on the grand ducal lands, with 30 and 36-morg voloks also allowed; no size is printed.
The entry gives the Arabic name as Ghuzat al-Jihad; the article has al-ghuzāt al-mujāhidīn. No Arabic name is printed.
Death date given as 4 April 314 in the article; the text keeps the year only.
Left out the Cartagena siege detail: the article's wording about whose supplies the English warships protected is unclear.
The entry says Thipchang defeated the Burmese governor of Lampang; the article says he shot 'the king, who commanded the Burmese army'. The text names neither.
The article dates the papyrus to 'the 1140s BCE' in one place and to around 1145 BCE (1140-1150) in another; the text gives no year beyond the 4th year of Ramesses V.

The article's lead says Charles I first granted him the governorship in 1642, while its body says he replaced Wyatt in 1641 (as the entry has it) and arrived at Jamestown in 1642; the text gives no year for the appointment.

The entry dates his policy from 1902; the article has his transfer in 1899 and his plan in 1901. These do not contradict, but the text keeps the article's years. The article does not name Tidjikja as the place of his death.
The entry says the Northern Qi emperors kept a residence nearby; the article does not mention it.
The entry says he raised the Beifu army at Jingkou from northern refugees; the article names neither.

The article contradicts itself on the song's origin: its lead says Fawzi composed it for the 1961 film El Hub Keda, but also that Azzam released it in 1960 and that it was very popular in the 1950s, and that an Ismail Yassin film of the 1950s featured it. The text does not say when or for what it was composed.

The article gives the move of the capital as 1272 and the building of the fortress as 1273, the period as capital as 1273-1284, and the rock's height as almost a hundred metres in one place and 90 m in another; the text gives none of these figures. The article spells the king Bhuvenakabahu and Buvanekabahu I, the entry Bhuvanaikabahu I; the text says 'the king'.
The entry calls him the last of the Shpata family; the article calls him the last Lord of Arta. The text says neither.
The entry says his descendants ruled until the city's destruction in the 16th century BCE; the article dates the end only by Hattusili I's conquest. The text gives no century.

Tholing: the entry says founded in 996, the article says built in 997; no year given in the text. The article gives his dates as c. 959-1040 and says he abdicated in c. 975 to become a lama, yet also that Tholing was built in 997 after he had been king for thirty years (self-contradictory); the entry has him a king who became a monk in the late 10th century. Lifespan and abdication date left out. The article places Tabo Monastery in Ladakh; location left out. The article says nothing of his captivity among the Qarluqs or of Atisha.

The article gives the proclamation of the East Hebei Autonomous Government as 15 November 1935, consistent with the entry; not repeated. Positions under the Wang Jingwei regime (Shanxi 1942, Legal Affairs Department from January 1944) condensed.

The article names the king 'Geumwa of Buyeo'; the entry says Eastern Buyeo. Written as King Geumwa without the state. The article's family list gives Buru of Buyeo as her son too; left out as it sits oddly with the legend told. 'Reception and legacy' chosen as the closest heading for a legendary figure's later worship.
The article gives the end of his reign as July 429; consistent with the entry, not repeated. The article does not name Shengle; the 423 attack is given only with the army's size.

The entry dates the creation of the special army to 1104 and the return of the fortresses to 1109; the article gives neither year but has Yejong order the withdrawal in 1108. The order is told without a year. The article says the war 'lasted for several years' after 1107; left out, as the entry has the fortresses returned in 1109.
The article gives his date of death as 14 April 572; consistent with the entry, not repeated. The article places Jinyang in 'modern Taiyuan, Shandong' (Taiyuan is in Shanxi); location left out.
The article says nothing of the mass burials or ritual deposits the entry mentions. 'Discovery and study' used for what the excavations show; the article has no present-day facts about the site.

The article says he took up his functions as sultan in February 1947, consistent with the entry's 1947. The entry says the sultanate was revived in 1999; the article says a titular sultan from another branch was chosen then. Not repeated.
Death and legacy section is short; its content (descendants) is all the article gives after his death.
The article gives his dates as 1156-1228 without 'c.'; the entry has c. 1156. The birth year is not repeated.

The article dates the mosaic to about the 2nd century while setting out the unresolved dating dispute (Flavian to Severan); no single date given in the text. The article does not mention lions and leopards supplied by the Garamantes or the trans-Saharan animal trade that the entry describes. The braided rope outlines and black backgrounds come from Kondoleon's description of the panels.

The entry dates the Battle of Mhlatuze River to 1819; the article to 1820. No year given in the text. The article's sentence on Zwide scattering 'the Mfekane tribe' is obscure; only the link to the Mfecane is kept. The article says nothing of Zwide's death in 1825 beyond the dates in its lead.

The entry says the assembly was held on 1 January 1527; the article says the nobles met on 31 December 1526 and agreed on Ferdinand on 1 January 1527. The meeting date is left out. The charter's list of signatories shortened to two names.

The entry speaks of taxes and trade restrictions; the article names only the boat tax and centralising measures. Not contradicted. The article does not say outright that he died in the Seychelles, only that he was exiled there 'where he died about 30 years later'; consistent with the entry.

SKIPPED: Article has under 250 words of substance: a short career list (medical studies, Hatay Maturity Society, Geneva delegation, parliamentary terms, Central Bank board, memoirs) that cannot fill 260 words without padding.
The entry says he captured the colony in February 1667; the article has him reach the river on 25 February and the English give up the whole colony on 6 March. The surrender date is left out.

The article says Saadi took his pen name in admiration of Abu Bakr and dedicated the Bustan to him; the entry says the pen name honoured the Salghurids and that the Bustan and Gulistan were dedicated to the dynasty. The pen name and dedications are left out. The entry speaks of submission to Ögedei; the article mentions only Hulagu Khan. Not contradicted.

The article's sentence on Stolpe Abbey ('at the side of Wartislaw I's assassination by a pagan in 1153') leaves unclear whether 1153 is the date of the killing or of the founding; the year is left out.

The article dates the predecessor company to 1877, while the entry says the company was founded in 1878; the text gives only the 1878 renaming. The entry dates the Karonga War 1887 to 1889; the article says the fighting ran from November 1886 to December 1887 and again from April 1888 to March 1889. The text avoids the start date and does not name the war.
The article gives his birth both as 'c. 1242' and as 1242; the text says about 1242.

The entry says about 800 left Abu Dhabi under Maktoum bin Butti and Obaid bin Said; the article gives no number and names only Maktoum bin Butti bin Sohal. Neither point is repeated. The article's material beyond the 1833 migration is mostly a list of rulers and members; living members are left out. The text is at the lower end of the length range.
